headline: Manasquan and Sea Bright rocks: bunker blitzes hold, bass bite thins in the heat
subhead: Bluefish are chewing through bait schools stacked tight against the jetties while stripers go quiet in the warm water — here's where the pattern's still paying off.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

First light on the Manasquan north jetty this week has looked the same every morning — a handful of regulars picking their way out over slick rock in the dark, headlamps bobbing, everybody watching the same thing: bunker pods stacked so thick against the rocks they turn the water black. That's the tell. When the bait's balled up tight like that, you don't need a fishfinder to know what's underneath it.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker-driven blitz would keep spreading north and south as long as the high pressure held and the bait stayed thick, and that's exactly what's playing out from Sea Bright down through Manasquan Inlet. Bluefish, mostly 3 to 6 pounds with some bigger cows mixed in, are hammering those bunker schools on the surface at first light and again in the last hour before dark. The pattern's simple: find the nervous water off the jetty tips, cast a metal-lip swimmer or a wide-wobble popper past the edge of the bait, and let the blues do the rest. Snagging live bunker on a treble and drifting it back on a fish-finder rig into the melee has been just as deadly for anybody who doesn't mind the extra rod work. Sea Bright's north jetty and the rocks off Monmouth Beach have both had bait pinned against them on the outgoing, and the Manasquan Inlet jetties — north side especially — have had blitzes break loose an hour either side of the tide change.

Stripers are a tougher conversation right now, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Ocean temps pushing into the mid-70s have shut most of the daytime bass activity down cold along this stretch. The fish haven't left — they've just gone nocturnal and gone deep. The move is working the jetty tips at true first light, before the sun gets on the water, targeting the deeper pockets where the rocks drop off fast — the outside corner of the Manasquan south jetty in 12 to 15 feet, or the deep slot off the third groin down from the Shark River Inlet north wall. Outgoing tide is doing the work, pulling bait and current together off the rock edges. Bottle plugs and Bomber long-lips fished slow along bottom have picked at a few slot fish in that window, and there's been better luck live-lining bunker on circle hooks for guys willing to fish through the blitz noise rather than around it — a lot of the bigger bass are shadowing the bluefish schools, picking off cripples. It's not the kind of bite where you fill a cooler. It's the kind where you put in the dawn hours and take one or two quality fish home, and call that a win in August.

Fluke have been the more dependable player this week, and the inlets are carrying the load. Shark River Inlet's channel edge, drifted on the last two hours of the outgoing into the first hour of slack, has produced a steady grade of fluke to 4 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked in 18 to 22 feet right along the deeper channel break. Manasquan Inlet's been similar — the stretch between the Coast Guard station and the railroad bridge has held fish on the drift, though boat traffic on weekends makes for a crowded program. Belmar's inside grounds off the Shark River have kicked out shorts mixed with keepers on strips of squid teamed with the Gulp for guys drifting slow with the tide rather than powering through it.

Porgies remain the honest bread-and-butter bite off just about every jetty from Sea Bright down to Spring Lake. Bloodworms and clam on bottom rigs fished tight to the rocks in 10 to 20 feet have kept rods bent all week, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slackens enough to hold bottom without getting swept into the structure. It's not glamorous, but it's the fish that'll save a slow morning when the blues and bass aren't cooperating, and there's been no shortage of them.

Sea conditions have been a factor worth respecting. Offshore buoy readings this week showed 3 to 4-foot seas running on a short 6-second period — that's a choppy, uncomfortable swell period, not a clean groundswell, and it's made footing on the outer rocks at Sea Bright and the Manasquan jetties sketchier than it looks from the beach. If you're jetty walking in the dark, that short-period slop is exactly the kind of stuff that catches you off guard on a wet rock. Fish the inside faces when it's running like that and save the exposed tips for calmer mornings.

Looking ahead, expect the bunker-and-bluefish pattern to keep running as long as this stable weather holds and the bait doesn't get pushed offshore by a wind shift. If a northeast blow comes through and scatters those pods, the blitzes will go quiet fast, so this window is worth working while it lasts. Stripers should improve incrementally as we push toward September and water temps start easing off — that's when the dawn bite historically extends past that first hour of light. And keep one eye out for the first false albacore push; it's early yet for this stretch, but the calendar's getting close, and when the bait starts thinning out along the beach in a couple weeks, that's usually the tell that the albies aren't far behind.
